transcript:
Header: 2026-07-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~55m
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood Solutions Eng); Liam (CTO), Priya (ML Lead), Marcus (Infra), Anya (SRE)
Link: [redwood/profiles/estrata-2026-07-14]

Summary (auto): technical deep dive, profiling artifacts shared, agreed next steps for bench on customer infra.

00:00 Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, we'll do a deep dive into GPU runtime profiling, tried to focus on what matters for your 2k token responses and vector search pipeline
00:22 Liam: hey thanks, quick note, Priya's going to share the model we're looking at - it's a trimmed 13B with custom fine-tune and attention tweaks
00:35 Maya: awesome, the agenda — kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM perf, cudagraphs capture strategies, kv cache sizing, batching heuristics, quantization experiments, and then open q&a
01:05 Marcus: just so you know, our infra is mostly A10G previews in lab, and for prod we have a mix of A100 and H100 in a private VPC - so on-prem-ish networking and strict egress rules
01:30 Jordan: that's helpful — we'll call out the VPC/on-prem constraints and how that affects model variants and fallback policies
02:10 Maya: jumping into profiler - first slide - kernel selection. so TensorRT-LLM will pick fused attention kernels and optimized matmuls, vLLM relies more on cuBLAS/cuDNN paths unless you plug in TRT kernels. in our internal tests we saw 15-30% token/sec improvement on 13B when TRT was available
02:50 Priya: does that change with sequence length? our typical is 2k but sometimes spikes to 4k for long docs
03:12 Maya: yes, kernel choice and memory layout matters a lot as sequence grows. TRT fused kernels often win for longer context because they reduce memory traffic; but the win depends on kv cache layout and batch shapes
03:45 Diego: note that vLLM's batching strategy is more workload-adaptive in our open builds - it will coalesce different sequence lengths more aggressively but you pay some latency tail for in-flight coalescing
04:10 Anya: can you clarify kv cache sizing — we saw OOMs when switching from 2k to 4k with 32GB cards
04:30 Maya: common pitfall — KV cache is per-token per-layer. doubling seq length roughly doubles KV memory. TRT sometimes allows quantized KV which reduces footprint but watch alignment and padding. for 32GB, with 13B and 4k you likely need 48+GB effective unless you quantize or shard KV across GPUs
05:05 Marcus: we saw better perf with tensor parallel sharding, but networking between nodes in our VPC adds ~200-300us — is there a recommended approach?
05:40 Jordan: two patterns - prefer model placement to avoid cross-node KV for low-latency paths, or accept cross-node for throughput and tune batching. autoscale burst pools can help for peaks but your private VPC egress and firewall mean we should test in your env
06:20 Priya: about CUDA graphs — we've been told they improve latency for steady batches, but capturing is flaky with dynamic shapes
06:45 Maya: correct. CUDA Graphs shine when you have predictable shapes and fixed batch sizes. capture time can be costly; for dynamic shapes we recommend a hybrid: capture for common pad shapes and fall back to streamed kernel paths for rare shapes. also watch warmup: initial tokens can be much slower during capture
07:20 Liam: any gotchas with cudagraphs and kv cache?
07:35 Maya: if your capture includes KV initialization it's fine, but if you capture with small context and then replay with larger context you can get incorrect indexing. capture must match runtime memory layout. we sometimes capture multiple graphs (e.g., 512, 1024, 2048) and switch at runtime — adds complexity but reduces tail latency
08:10 Diego: on quantization — int8 vs 4-bit. int8 with per-channel scales in TRT looks OK for some workloads but degrades certain instruction-following behaviors. 4-bit (nf4, GPTQ style) gives much smaller memory but needs dequantization on host side for some ops which costs cycles
08:50 Priya: how do you validate quality regressions from quant? we have internal evals and rouge/bleu-ish metrics but it's noisy
09:15 Maya: recommend a small eval suite keyed to your top-30 prompts. run side-by-side perf and quality; Redwood Optimize suggests thresholds and automatic regression alerts. practical approach: run a 5k example set and compute similarity metrics plus sampling-based human checks for high-risk prompts
09:50 Marcus: for vLLM we saw better early-latency on small batches but worse throughput at saturation vs TRT, is that expected?
10:10 Maya: yes — vLLM's scheduler is optimized for low-latency single-session workloads by preempting and coalescing; TensorRT-LLM with TRT kernels tends to excel at sustained throughput once warmed and with heavy quantization. tradeoff: TRT requires more upfront compile/capture time and is less flexible for dynamic shapes
11:00 Luna (Speaker mislabeled): [crosstalk] sorry, my mic — are there differences in failure modes?
11:20 Jordan: good question — TRT pipelines can fail faster on unsupported ops during model changes; vLLM is more forgiving but can have higher latencies under heavy tail. both need good canary tests before rollout
12:00 Priya: can you walk through a sample config you'd recommend for our A100 fleet with 2k typical length?
12:15 Maya: sure — high-level: prefer TRT-LLM for prod throughput on A100 with int8/gptq where accuracy is acceptable. pipeline: 1) compile TRT with representative 512/1024/2048 shapes, 2) capture cudagraphs for the common shapes, 3) enable prefix KV caching for frequent prompts, 4) set batching policy: burst window 25ms, max batch 16 for latency-sensitive routes, throughput routes allow larger batches. also set a fallback to vLLM variant for highly dynamic or unsupported ops
13:05 Marcus: about caching — we have many repeated prefixes in chatbot flows, how effective is prefix/KV caching?
13:25 Maya: very effective — if 40% of requests share a common 256-token prefix, you can reduce token compute by roughly that amount. but cache hit rates depend on prompt normalization and session affinity. watch memory growth and eviction policies
14:00 Priya: what about security for private deployments — KMS and audit logs — any perf hits?
14:20 Jordan: KMS calls are outside the token path; for inference we use short-lived encryption keys or hardware HSM to minimize runtime overhead. audit logging adds IO but you can buffer and batch logs to avoid token path latency effects
15:00 Liam: can we get a quick walkthrough of a profiling artifact you mentioned?
15:10 Maya: sure, I uploaded a profile - you'll see a timeline where TRT kernels (fused attn) show long contiguous GPU usage and lower kernel dispatch overhead; vLLM shows more frequent small kernels. here - I'll share link now [link to profiling traces]
15:45 Priya: we're also doing multi-tenant inference — how do you isolate QoS?
16:00 Diego: we recommend resource pools and router-level SLO prioritization; for private you can pin certain models to dedicated GPU pools and throttle best-effort jobs. Redwood Dedicated supports capacity partitions and autoscale thresholds
16:40 Marcus: any tips on reducing memory overhead without quantizing?
16:55 Maya: sharded KV, rotary embedding pruning for long context (trim unused kv rows), and mixed-precision BF16 where supported. also offload rarely used layers to CPU for very long contexts but that hurts latency
17:30 Priya: we occasionally do on-prem air-gapped deployments, is there anything special for cudagraphs/trt?
17:50 Jordan: ensure you have the exact CUDA/cuDNN/TensorRT stack versions used for capture on the target machines; cudagraphs may fail if driver versions differ. we recommend a containerized runtime with pinned libs and an integration test harness to validate captures post-deploy
18:40 Liam: let's talk numbers — in your experiments what's typical tail latency reduction with multiple graph captures vs none?
19:00 Maya: in a Redwood internal 13B test on H100, median token latency reduced ~20% with graphs captured and warmed, p95 improved ~30-40% when you used multiple graph shapes and fast switching. but cold-starts during recompile or capture can be seconds, so warmup is essential
20:00 Priya: and throughput gains?
20:15 Maya: throughput measured in tokens/sec went up 1.3-1.6x for TRT compiled int8 paths vs baseline vLLM in our runs, but that depends on quant quality and batch size. with larger batches TRT sees bigger wins
21:00 Marcus: are there orchestration concerns with switching graphs at runtime?
21:20 Diego: yes: you need a small state machine mapping request shape to graph id, and safe fallback when graph switch fails. Redwood runtime includes graph manager in our Dedicated release that handles this gracefully and falls back to interpreter path
22:05 Priya: curious about monitoring — what metrics should we add to SLOs?
22:20 Maya: token latency distribution (median/p95/p99), GPU util by kernel type, graph-switch rate/failures, kv cache hit rate, memory headroom, dequant/quant error metrics, and request-level accuracy deltas post-quant.
notes: Occasional transcription errors: vLLM sometimes transcribed as v-l m or vll m, crosstalk labeled as 'Luna' once. References to shared artifacts: profiling traces link, runbook snippet, sample config yaml. Customer emphasized private VPC constraints and A100/H100 fleet.
